strengths: The paper introduces a potentially useful descriptive tool: closed-form Gaussian optimal-transport alignment followed by a normalized distributional residual, collected into layerwise signatures. Comparing architectures through their activation behavior is relevant to understanding vision models beyond depth and parameter count.

The empirical survey is substantial, covering CNNs, architectures obtained through neural architecture search, and transformers using all 50,000 ImageNet validation images. The raw signatures and controlled comparison of ResNet20 with and without residual connections provide interesting evidence of architecture-dependent patterns.

The supplementary material provides useful supporting analysis, including an analytical ReLU example, covariance-estimation experiments, batch-size and nine-seed checks for VGG16, additional input datasets, and comparisons across training methods. A code repository is linked.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a theoretically sound measure of activation non-linearity is not established. Equation (5) discards input-output correspondence and can assign maximum affinity to a nonlinear activation. For X uniformly distributed on [-1,1] and σ(x)=|x|, both σ(X) and T_aff(X)=(X+1)/2 are uniform on [0,1], so the score is exactly 1. Corollary 3.2 and Theorem 3.3 establish properties under positive-definite linear-map assumptions; they do not establish the general identification claimed in Section 3.1. This is a material limitation of the proposed interpretation.

The connection between activation signatures and whole-network non-linearity remains insufficiently validated. The reported ViT signatures measure GELU activations while omitting nonlinear operations in attention and layer normalization. Composition and cancellation across layers also affect the resulting function. Without a theoretical relationship or independent empirical validation against network-level functional complexity, the results support differences in activation statistics more strongly than the claims about transformers' expressive power or overall non-linearity.

The accuracy analysis in Figure 6 is exploratory. The paper selects the best statistic separately for each architecture family and evaluates fitted relationships on the same small collections of models, including only five ViTs. There is no held-out evaluation or assessment of the uncertainty introduced by statistic selection and nonlinear fitting. Consequently, the reported correlations do not establish reliable predictive advantages over model size, depth, or compute, and do not isolate non-linearity from architectural and training differences.

Several arguments used to dismiss alternatives are technically incorrect. Remark 3.6 calls T_aff a globally optimal nonlinear mapping, although it is affine and its transport optimality concerns the Gaussian approximations. Ordinary least squares with an intercept has training R² in [0,1], so the stated unboundedness objection does not apply to that baseline. Section 3.3 also dismisses Jacobian-based measures for ReLU networks despite their almost-everywhere differentiability. Low Pearson correlations in Table 1 establish disagreement between metrics, but do not establish which metric better measures non-linearity or provides additional useful information.

The practical estimator is not adequately connected to the theoretical construction. Appendix C describes spatial averaging as lossless, although averaging generally destroys information and the averaged post-activation tensor is not the activation of the averaged input. Figure 9's illustrative comparison does not establish preservation across the studied architectures. Covariance shrinkage also changes the exact moment-matching construction, while the manuscript does not establish preservation of its guarantees. The numerical Wasserstein solver and treatment of zero-variance outputs, for which Equation (5) is undefined, are insufficiently specified. These issues affect both interpretation and reproducibility.
